full_text_en:
Gansu Rare Earth Company v. Gannan Normal College Mineral Products Processing Plant — Dispute over Rare Earth Purchase Contract (Retrial Application)

Applicant for Retrial: Gansu Rare Earth Company.

The applicant for retrial, Gansu Rare Earth Company, dissatisfied with the final judgment of the Jiangxi High People's Court in the case of dispute over a purchase contract between Gannan Normal College Mineral Products Processing Plant and it, filed an application for retrial with the Supreme People's Court pursuant to Article 178 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC.

The facts found and the judgment results of the first and second instance trials in this case:

Ganlong Joint Venture Rare Earth Company (hereinafter referred to as Ganlong Company) was a closely integrated mixed oxide rare earth production enterprise established in 1985 by Gansu Rare Earth Company and Jiangxi Gan County Rare Earth Company for the joint development of rare earth resources in Gan County. According to the joint venture agreement, the manager was appointed by Gansu Rare Earth Company.

On January 7, 1989, Ganlong Company, acting as agent for Gansu Rare Earth Company, entered into a contract with Gannan Normal College Mineral Products Processing Plant (hereinafter referred to as the Processing Plant) for the purchase and sale of 30 tons of europium-enriched rare earth. This contract had been performed, and after settlement, Gansu Rare Earth Company still owed the Processing Plant RMB 15,466.2.

On April 6, 1989, the former manager of Ganlong Company, Qu Sanyuan, together with the new manager, Qian Guangxiang, and deputy manager, Li Peijin, among others, made a courtesy visit to the Processing Plant for the handover between the outgoing and incoming management. During the conversation, Qian Guangxiang and others mentioned that Gansu Rare Earth Company urgently needed to purchase 30 tons of europium-enriched rare earth. The Processing Plant indicated that it then had 25 tons, with several more tons being calcined. Subsequently, an oral agreement was reached for the purchase and sale of 30 tons of rare earth. On April 8, Qian Guangxiang sent Li Peijin and others to the Processing Plant to sign a contract for the purchase and sale of 30 tons of rare earth based on the orally agreed terms of April 6. The contract stipulated: a unit price of RMB 48,000 per ton; delivery at the supplier's warehouse; and completion of delivery before April 20. The contract also contained provisions on product specifications, quality standards, inspection methods, settlement methods, and liability for breach. The validity period of the contract was from April 8, 1989, to July 30, 1989. The contract was signed and sealed in the same manner as the contract of January 7, i.e., the purchaser was Gansu Rare Earth Company, and the contract was affixed with the special contract seal of Ganlong Company (acting as agent). On the day the contract was signed, Ganlong Company sent a telegram to Gansu Rare Earth Company stating: "Contract for 30 tons of europium-rich ore signed, delivery before April 20, unit price RMB 48,000 per ton, payment terms: RMB 500,000 by end of April, another RMB 500,000 before May 15, balance paid in full before June 30, overdue interest at 1.1% per month. Please remit previous payment promptly." On April 10, Gansu Rare Earth Company sent a telegram to Ganlong Company: "Price is too high, do not deliver for now. Current Guangdong price is RMB 46,000, processing." On April 11, Ganlong Company informed the Processing Plant of the contents of Gansu Rare Earth Company's telegram. The Processing Plant indicated that the price could be negotiated further. On April 14, the Processing Plant sent a telegram to Gansu Rare Earth Company: "Goods ready, please prepare payment and take delivery, remit previous payment promptly." On April 15 and 16, Ganlong Company and the Processing Plant negotiated on the contract price. The Processing Plant again indicated that the price could be negotiated, but the parties failed to reach an agreement. On April 20, Gansu Rare Earth Company and Ganlong Company did not go to the Processing Plant to take samples, conduct inspections, or take delivery as stipulated in the contract. On May 4, Qu Sanyuan returned to Gansu and, at the request of the Processing Plant before leaving Jiangxi, reported the contract signing to Gansu Rare Earth Company. On May 19, Qu Sanyuan, acting on the instructions of Gansu Rare Earth Company, sent a telegram to the Processing Plant: "Due to hydrochloric acid shortage, production halted. Europium-rich ore not needed for now. Please dispose of the 30 tons yourselves." On the same day, Gansu Rare Earth Company sent a telegram to Ganlong Company: "Due to hydrochloric acid shortage, production halted. Europium-rich ore not needed for now. Have notified the Processing Plant to handle it." After receiving Qu Sanyuan's telegram, the Processing Plant sent telegrams to Gansu Rare Earth Company and Qu Sanyuan on May 20 and 21 respectively: "We have processed 30 tons of europium-rich rare earth according to contract specifications; 90% of the total cannot be exported. Please find a solution to avoid greater economic losses" and "The 30 tons of rare earth were specially prepared for you; who bears the economic losses?" Gansu Rare Earth Company did not reply. On May 22, Gansu Rare Earth Company telegraphed Ganlong Company: "Processing Plant has urged twice about europium-rich ore. Please handle properly. Need yttrium-rich ore (another mineral unrelated to this case)." On May 23, Ganlong Company telegraphed Gansu Rare Earth Company: "Visited Processing Plant; they agreed to ship yttrium-rich ore, but require someone to bring RMB 200,000 before shipping..." On May 26, Ganlong Company again telegraphed Gansu Rare Earth Company: "Relations strained with Processing Plant over 30-ton rare earth contract. Today they notified that with RMB 200,000 only 5 tons can be shipped. If you want, remit funds." On June 17 of the same year, the Processing Plant wrote to Gansu Rare Earth Company, proposing negotiation to resolve the dispute over the 30-ton europium-rich ore contract and enclosing the contract of April 8. On June 26, Gansu Rare Earth Company replied to the Processing Plant: "Before receiving your letter, we were unaware the problem remained unresolved. Our company will accept 10 tons of yttrium-rich ore. As for the europium-rich ore, please dispose of it or negotiate a solution based on market prices after production resumes in August." After receiving the letter, the Processing Plant wrote to Gansu Rare Earth Company on July 15, stating that it could not dispose of the ore. Gansu Rare Earth Company did not reply. After the contract period expired, due to the accumulation of europium-rich ore, difficulties in capital turnover, and the need to improve quality standards to reduce losses, the Processing Plant had to reprocess the batch of europium-rich ore and resold it separately from August 3 to October 28. Due to changes in the rare earth market and other factors, it sustained economic losses of RMB 618,556.87. In August and November of the same year, Gansu Rare Earth Company sent Zhang Fuhai and Qu Sanyuan, respectively, to the Processing Plant twice to negotiate the aftermath of the purchase contract for 30 tons of europium-rich ore. Due to significant differences, no agreement was reached. On April 16, 1990, the Processing Plant filed a lawsuit with the Ganzhou Intermediate People's Court of Jiangxi Province, requesting that Gansu Rare Earth Company be ordered to compensate for all economic losses. Subsequently, it also requested that Gansu Rare Earth Company repay the outstanding debt under the January 7 contract.

The Ganzhou Intermediate People's Court held: Ganlong Company, acting on the instructions of Gansu Rare Earth Company, signed the contract in question with the Processing Plant in the name of Gansu Rare Earth Company. After the contract was signed, Ganlong Company promptly informed Gansu Rare Earth Company of the main terms of the contract by telegram. Gansu Rare Earth Company did not object to the contract signed by Ganlong Company in its name, except to indicate that the price was too high and requested no delivery for the time being. Moreover, in past business dealings, the Processing Plant and Gansu Rare Earth Company had concluded transactions in the same form. Therefore, it was confirmed that the contract signed by Ganlong Company on behalf of Gansu Rare Earth Company with the Processing Plant was valid. Gansu Rare Earth Company's failure to perform its obligations under the contract constituted a breach of contract; it bore full responsibility for the economic losses caused. The outstanding debt from previous business should also be repaid. Ganlong Company had duly performed its agency duties and was not at fault in the agency process. Based on this, the court ordered: 1. Termination of the performance of the contract signed by Ganlong Company on behalf of Gansu Rare Earth Company with the Processing Plant; 2. Gansu Rare Earth Company to pay liquidated damages of RMB 72,000 to the Processing Plant; 3. Gansu Rare Earth Company to pay compensation of RMB 546,556.87 to the Processing Plant; 4. Gansu Rare Earth Company to repay the outstanding debt of RMB 15,466.20 to the Processing Plant, plus interest of RMB 2,028.64.

Dissatisfied with the first instance judgment, Gansu Rare Earth Company appealed to the Jiangxi High People's Court, arguing that it had only orally asked Ganlong Company to look into the rare earth market and had not authorized it to sign the contract in question with the Processing Plant on its behalf. The court upon trial held that the facts were clear and the first instance court's finding that an agency relationship existed was correct. It dismissed the appeal of Gansu Rare Earth Company and affirmed the first instance judgment.

Dissatisfied with the final judgment of the Jiangxi High People's Court, Gansu Rare Earth Company applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial, alleging: Gansu Rare Earth Company only asked Ganlong Company to understand the market conditions and did not authorize it to sign the contract in question. Ganlong Company did not obtain a power of attorney or letter of introduction from Gansu Rare Earth Company; Gansu Rare Earth Company also did not subsequently ratify the contract, nor was the contract performed; Ganlong Company's act of signing the contract in question beyond its authority should be borne by itself. After Gansu Rare Earth Company indicated that the price was too high, the Processing Plant expressed willingness to renegotiate, but the parties never agreed on a price, so the contract terminated on its own.

The Supreme People's Court upon review held: In the contract signed by Ganlong Company with the Processing Plant on April 8, 1989, the purchaser was named as Gansu Rare Earth Company, with the seal of Ganlong Company affixed—this was a form of manifestation of an agency relationship. By accepting this method of signing the contract, Ganlong Company indicated that it considered itself authorized by Gansu Rare Earth Company. On the same day the contract was signed, Ganlong Company sent a telegram to Gansu Rare Earth Company, detailing the content of the contract, rather than asking whether Gansu Rare Earth Company wanted the goods. This showed that Ganlong Company was not signing the contract as a purchaser and then making an offer to Gansu Rare Earth Company as a seller, but rather as an agent reporting on the agency matter to the principal. Regarding the telegram sent by Gansu Rare Earth Company on April 10 stating "Price is too high, do not deliver for now," when the first instance court investigated, it was confirmed by testimony that "We asked Ganlong Company not to deliver for now because we were afraid that after using up the Guangdong goods, we might still need them," which was an expression of intention to postpone delivery. This telegram did not clearly express that Rare Earth Company denied Ganlong Company's act of agency in this contract. Subsequently, the telegram from the Processing Plant to Gansu Rare Earth Company on April 14 stating "Goods ready, please prepare payment and take delivery," the report by Qu Sanyuan to Gansu Rare Earth Company upon returning from Jiangxi in early May about the contract signing, the multiple exchanges of telegrams among the three parties from May 19 to May 26, the letter from Gansu Rare Earth Company to the Processing Plant on June 26, 1989, and the fact that Gansu Rare Earth Company sent personnel twice to handle the aftermath—all indicated that Gansu Rare Earth Company did not clearly deny Ganlong Company's act of signing the contract in question with the Processing Plant in the name of Gansu Rare Earth Company. The fact that Gansu Rare Earth Company indicated the price was too high and the Processing Plant said it could be renegotiated, but no price was agreed upon, was raised after Ganlong Company signed the contract in question on behalf of Gansu Rare Earth Company and constituted a request to modify the contract. Pursuant to Article 28 of the Economic Contract Law of the PRC, before the parties reach a new agreement, the original contract remains valid; there was no issue of automatic termination. According to Article 66(1) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, which provides, "If a person knows that another person is carrying out civil acts in his name and does not deny it, it shall be deemed as consent," the finding that an agency relationship existed in this case was correct. Gansu Rare Earth Company's failure to perform the contract in question constituted a breach of contract, and it should bear civil liability for the losses caused by its breach. Accordingly, pursuant to Article 179(2) of the Civil Procedure Law, on December 20, 1991, the Supreme People's Court dismissed the retrial application of Gansu Rare Earth Company.
